notes.short: Believers' death is called falling asleep
notes.about: Paul says that Jesus died; believers who have died he calls those who have fallen asleep in Him. Death is named gently as sleep, for God will bring them with Jesus: for those in Him, death will end in rising, as sleep ends in waking.

figure.name: Euphemism
figure.means: died: death spoken of gently, as a sleep from which God will raise them

original.note: In Paul's Greek the word for Jesus is apethanen, died; for believers it is koimēthentes, laid to sleep.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Euphemy: God calls His people asleep, since the Lord will come to wake them. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) notes that death is said of Christ but sleep of believers. A. J. Mason (Ellicott) finds the metaphor of sleep sweetening the phrase. Barnes calls it a most beautiful expression for rest in hope of waking; Calvin and Clarke read it as death in Christ.
notes.limit: Some take the word sleep as set on purpose against the word died used of Jesus. The note does not take the sleep to mean that the dead know nothing until the resurrection.

cites.quote: in the case of His own people, He speaks of their being “put to sleep by Jesus” (1Th 4:14 ). It is only a “sleep”; because the Lord Himself will come to wake them.

cites.quote: He died and then rose: so believers shall die and then rise with Him. But in His case death is the term used, Co1 15:3 , Co1 15:6 , &c.; in theirs, sleep; because His death has taken for them the sting from death.

cites.quote: To sleep in Christ, is to retain in death the connection that we have with Christ, for those that are by faith ingrafted into Christ, have death in common with him, that they may be partakers with him of life.

Which sleep in Jesus - A most beautiful expression. It is not merely that they have calm repose - like a gentle slumber - in the hope of awaking again ... Such is the sleep of our pious friends now in the grave; such will be our own when we die.

notes.short: The Day comes “like a thief in the night”
notes.about: Paul says the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night: suddenly and without warning, on those who feel safe. Then he turns the picture: believers are not in the darkness, so that day should not overtake them like a thief. Jesus used the same picture in Matthew 24:43.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: like a thief in the night
figure.means: the Lord's coming in judgment, sudden and unlooked for, taking by surprise those who are careless and unready

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a similitude: the day will come suddenly on unbelievers and take them by surprise, as though asleep. Barnes says the point of the comparison is that it comes without warning, as a robber breaks into a house. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says the apostles take the image from their Lord's parable; Mason (Ellicott) calls it a simile often used in the apostles' teaching.
notes.limit: In verse 4 two of the oldest manuscripts read thieves rather than thief, and scholars differ on the reading.

cites.quote: Here we have an explanation of the similitude, the day of the Lord will be like a thief in the night. Why so? because it will come suddenly to unbelievers, when not looked for, so that it will take them by surprise, as though they were asleep.

As a thief in the night - Suddenly and unexpectedly, as a robber breaks into a dwelling. A thief comes without giving any warning, or any indications of his approach. ... In this way the Lord Jesus will return to judgment ... If this be not the point of the comparison in expressions like this, what is it?

cites.quote: as a thief in the night--The apostles in this image follow the parable of their Lord, expressing how the Lord's coming shall take men by surprise ( Mat 24:43 ; Pe2 3:10 ). ... The thief not only gives no notice of his approach but takes all precaution to prevent the household knowing of it. So the Lord ( Rev 16:15 ).

cites.quote: As a thief in the night — i.e. unexpectedly ( Mat 24:43 ), and under cover of darkness. The frequency of the simile (see references) throws light on the words “know perfectly,” making it apparent that it was the ordinary formula in which the doctrine was universally taught by the Apostles.
